item.title: How should I go about interpretting extended PGLS results for Species effects?
item.dc:creator: Mike Collyer
item.description:
What is extended PGLS?

Phylogenetic generalized least squares (PGLS) might invoke varied impressions for what is involved but it is really simple in concept. Least squares is a process of parameter estimation, which minimizes the sum of squared (vector lengths of) residuals. This is often revealed with the equation:

for the estimation of coefficients, , given some model, , and data, . One might think the equation looks a lot like a matrix form of this:

which if and were mean-centered is the definition of a slope.

Generalized least-squares (GLS) recognizes that and are maybe not appropriate, as is. If we transformed and in some way, i.e., , and , then we would have:

Pretty simple, right? So, in matrix form, this concept is:

What makes P-GLS a specific GLS method is that the transformation is based on expected phylogenetic relatedness (non-independence) from a Brownian motion (BM) model of evolutionary divergence; i.e., species more closely related should have more similar traits.

The transformation that makes the equation above is found thusly:

where is the phylogenetic covariance matrix from a BM model of evolutionary divergence. is the square-root matrix of the inverse of . Transformations are made as:

these transformed matrices are used to estimate .

What does the “extended” part of extended-PGLS mean?

above is for species. If we have observations, where becasue we sampeld more individuals than 1 per species, we could extend via:

where is a model matrix with dummy variable to indicate to which species each observation belongs. is an matrix that extends inter-species covariances to inter-individual locations in the larger matrix.

But this is problematic!

Such a matrix is singular and will not easily allow estimation of . We can attempt to make it non-singular by further weighting covariances, to allow observations to be slightly more independent than we would expect based on species, because of inter-individual variation. Here is how we can do that:

is a weight matrix (diagonal matrix) providing values to use to jointly multiply the products between and , to lessen their magnitude. The elements of are equal to:

The parameter, is an independence parameter. If 0, then the weights are 1, meaning the transformation is unweighted. Larger values push the weights toward 0, making covariance small, meaning a trend toward independece of observations. The parameter, is a sample size adjuster. If , sample size has no effect on weights. If based on sample size, then weights are decreased in proportion to the square-root of sample size, allowing larger samples to behave as if more independent.

In (Adams & Collyer, 2024), we used and adjusted for sample size. We did this to accommodate the ill-conditioned covariance matrix produced by using . But let’s see what we could have learned by varying .

Varying in the pupfish.ws example

Here is basically what we presented in (Adams & Collyer, 2024).

library(geomorph)
data(pupfish.ws)

fit <- extended.pgls(
  f1 = coords~Species * Sex + Population, 
  data = pupfish.ws, 
  species = "Species",
  phy = pupfish.ws$phy,
  delta = 0.1, 
  print.progress = FALSE)
      
LRT <- lr_test(fit, print.progress = FALSE)   
LRT
                  Wilks        LR         Z  pval
Species     0.470155560  731.2960  6.143384 0.001
Sex         0.894646636  107.8752  2.760067 0.005
Population  0.022496534 3676.7635 27.420145 0.001
Species:Sex 0.420985377  838.3371 10.581099 0.001
Full.Model  0.005167624 5102.0980 24.553456 0.001

What if we used different values of ?

deltas <- seq(0.05, 0.5, 0.05)

This is a good point to go get a coffee or a beer, maybe a light meal, if doing this on a standard computer.

Result <- lapply(as.list(deltas), function(d){
  fit <- extended.pgls(
  f1 = coords~Species * Sex + Population, 
  data = pupfish.ws, 
  species = "Species",
  phy = pupfish.ws$phy,
  delta = d, 
  print.progress = FALSE)
  
  LRT <- lr_test(fit, print.progress = FALSE)
  LRT
})

Now, let’s make a graph!

Z_scores <- t(sapply(Result, function(x) x$tab$Z))
colnames(Z_scores) <- rownames(LRT$tab)

plot(deltas, Z_scores[, 1], pch = 16,
     col = "#9E9E9E", type = "o",
     ylim = c(min(Z_scores), max(Z_scores)),
     xlab = "delta", ylab = "Z")
abline(h = 0, lty = 3)
points(deltas, Z_scores[, 2],pch = 17,
     col = "#A26060", type = "o")
points(deltas, Z_scores[, 3],pch = 18,
     col = "#9F6785", type = "o")
points(deltas, Z_scores[, 4],pch = 19,
     col = "#3E2C53", type = "o")
points(deltas, Z_scores[, 5],pch = 20,
     col = "#46686B", type = "o")
      
legend("bottom",
       rownames(LRT$tab),
       lty = 1, pch = 16:20,
       col = c("#9E9E9E","#A26060", "#9F6785",
               "#3E2C53", "#46686B"),
       bty = "n")

What did we learn?

  1. Only Species is largely affected by changing . This makes some sense, since covariances are based on species relatedness, and augments these values at the individual level.
  2. Small changes in effect sizes were apparent for non-species effects, only where . Mostly this was the case for the full model, which contains Species.
  3. Otherwise, effects were consistent, irrespective of .
  4. All effects were stable at
  5. Species was a significant effect at

How do we interpret this?

First, cautiously! Is small or large? Does the fact that Species behaves as if independent at suggest that even with a large amount of phylogenetic relevance (because , meaning this is not a large change from a weight of 1 ) the species effect is still large?

Second, because the Species effect is not as much interest as the Species:Sex effect in a study like this, does it matter? The effect size is consistent for the latter effect, regardless of .

If I were to report these results again, here is what I would do:

  1. Remove the Species effect from the table. It is not helpful.
  2. Report the trend for the Species effect based on a range of , separate from the other effects in the table.
  3. Speculate whether the low value is consistent with an adaptive radiation. If a significant Species effect is observed even if the linear model is rigged to account for it, it suggests species might diverge in shape more than expected from a BM model of divergence.
  4. Focus interpretations on Species:Sex. This is the point of the analysis, anyway, and it appears scaling weights to deal with the awkward non-species-effect that could arise has no influence on differences of within-species trends across species!

References

Adams, D. C., & Collyer, M. L. (2024). Extending phylogenetic regression models for comparing within-species patterns across the tree of life. Methods in Ecology and Evolution, 15(12), 2234–2246. doi:10.1111/2041-210X.14438

item.title: Should I adjust my P-values for pairwise comparisons in permutation tests?
item.dc:creator: Mike Collyer
item.description:
What does it mean to adjust -values?

It is well known that multiple tests using the same significance level will have inflated type I error rates. We can look to the binomial probability distribution to appreciate this. If , and one performs, e.g., 10 pairwise tests of mean differences, then the probability of not committing a type I error for any test assuming the probability for any test is is actually . This means the probability of at least one type I error is . There is a 40% chance of making a type I error in at least one of the tests, assuming a risk of a 5% error rate for each test. This is scary.

So what to do?

There are generally two ways to approach this and each way has its variants (not discussed in detail here). One (and the one I prefer for reason that will become obvious) is adjust the pairwise level of significance, . For example, one might decide that if the experimentwise , then the pairwise . Therefore, one would not reject the null hypothesis that means are equal unless a pairwise test statistic has a threshold of a 0.5% probability of occurrence (equal or greater) in a sampling distribution of the statistic.

The other is to adjust the -value. If the -value for the test is and there are ten tests performed, then the -value becomes (or , whichever is smaller).

it should be clear that these two procedures are exactly the same concept (called Bonferroni correction). Whether shifting or shifting , they are shifted toward each other, making a test more conservative for rejection of the null hypothesis. (Note the Bonferroni correction is very conservative but other methods are less so. Some might even order -values and become progressively more conservative with additional tests.)

So why has RRPP not had an ability to adjust -values with the pairwise function?

Actually, a quick announcement, starting with version 2.2.1, the pairwise function does have this capability. But we do not recommend using it. We have reluctantly added it because other R functions have it, and we want users to have options, but its use is fraught with potential inferential errors. To demonstrate, let’s look at an example with the Pupfish data.

library(RRPP)
Pupfish$Group <- interaction(Pupfish$Sex, Pupfish$Pop)
system.time(fit1 <- lm.rrpp(coords ~ Group, 
                           data = Pupfish,
                           turbo = FALSE,
                           verbose = TRUE,
                           Parallel = TRUE,
                           iter = 49999))
   user  system elapsed 
 23.119  25.354  17.043 
system.time(PW1 <- pairwise(fit1, 
                  groups = Pupfish$Group))
   user  system elapsed 
  7.109   0.105   7.278 
S1 <- summary(PW1, stat.table = FALSE)
S1$pairwise.tables$P 
           F.Marsh M.Marsh F.Sinkhole M.Sinkhole
F.Marsh      1e+00 0.00002    0.00008    0.00002
M.Marsh      2e-05 1.00000    0.00002    0.00154
F.Sinkhole   8e-05 0.00002    1.00000    0.00496
M.Sinkhole   2e-05 0.00154    0.00496    1.00000

The example shows just the -values, to reduce the amount of output printed. This informs us that every group means is significantly different from every other, even if we adjust to be .

If we instead adjust the -values, we get the following:

S1a <- summary(PW1, stat.table = FALSE,
               test.type = "stdist",
              p.adjust.method = "bonferroni")
S1a$pairwise.tables$P 
           F.Marsh M.Marsh F.Sinkhole M.Sinkhole
F.Marsh    1.00000 0.00012    0.00012    0.00012
M.Marsh    0.00012 1.00000    0.00012    0.00024
F.Sinkhole 0.00012 0.00012    1.00000    0.00036
M.Sinkhole 0.00012 0.00024    0.00036    1.00000

We still reject every pairwise null hypotheis because all adjusted -values are less than 0.05. But notice that we used permutations, which meant waiting a half-minute for results. If we were not so patient, we might do something like this:

system.time(fit2 <- lm.rrpp(coords ~ Group, 
                            data = Pupfish,
                            turbo = FALSE,
                            verbose = TRUE,
                            Parallel = TRUE,
                            iter = 499))
   user  system elapsed 
  0.164   0.218   0.194 
system.time(PW2 <- pairwise(fit2, 
                            groups = Pupfish$Group))
   user  system elapsed 
  0.064   0.004   0.069 
S2a <- summary(PW2, stat.table = FALSE,
               test.type = "stdist",
              p.adjust.method = "bonferroni")
S2a$pairwise.tables$P 
           F.Marsh M.Marsh F.Sinkhole M.Sinkhole
F.Marsh      1.000   0.012      0.012      0.012
M.Marsh      0.012   1.000      0.012      0.012
F.Sinkhole   0.012   0.012      1.000      0.012
M.Sinkhole   0.012   0.012      0.012      1.000

This changes things! (We probably would not use only 500 permutations but it helps to illustrate a point.) We got quick results but they are not the same results.

Now, let’s re-summarize the results choosing not to adjust -values but instead adjust the level of significance (confidence).

S2 <- summary(PW2, stat.table = TRUE,
              test.type = "stdist",
               p.adjust.method = "none",
              confidence = 1 - 0.05/6)
S2

Pairwise comparisons

Groups: F.Marsh M.Marsh F.Sinkhole M.Sinkhole 

RRPP: 500 permutations

LS means:
Vectors hidden (use show.vectors = TRUE to view)

Pairwise standardized distances between means, plus statistics
P-values adjustment: none 
                             d UCL (99.1666666666667%)        Z Pr > d
F.Marsh:M.Marsh       5.221816                1.801562 5.563939  0.002
F.Marsh:F.Sinkhole    3.656449                2.106903 3.671787  0.002
F.Marsh:M.Sinkhole    4.395133                1.987001 4.364833  0.002
M.Marsh:F.Sinkhole    4.863848                1.815198 5.313275  0.002
M.Marsh:M.Sinkhole    3.020484                1.888204 3.838870  0.002
F.Sinkhole:M.Sinkhole 2.712760                1.997251 3.030542  0.002

This might not seem that different but regardless of -value, we get to see the upper confidence limit associated with an adjusted . If we do not look at the -values, we see that the confidence limits are around a standardized . (Yes, these distances should feel like -statistics, as that is what they mimic.) All of the pairwise statistics are this large or larger. Let’s go back to our original permutation example and do the same thing.

S1 <- summary(PW1, stat.table = TRUE,
              test.type = "stdist",
              p.adjust.method = "none",
              confidence = 1 - 0.05/6)
S1

Pairwise comparisons

Groups: F.Marsh M.Marsh F.Sinkhole M.Sinkhole 

RRPP: 50000 permutations

LS means:
Vectors hidden (use show.vectors = TRUE to view)

Pairwise standardized distances between means, plus statistics
P-values adjustment: none 
                             d UCL (99.1666666666667%)        Z Pr > d
F.Marsh:M.Marsh       5.221816                1.945945 4.824779  2e-05
F.Marsh:F.Sinkhole    3.656449                1.932530 3.993549  2e-05
F.Marsh:M.Sinkhole    4.395133                1.936772 4.447712  2e-05
M.Marsh:F.Sinkhole    4.863848                1.957504 4.622671  2e-05
M.Marsh:M.Sinkhole    3.020484                1.948717 3.429291  4e-05
F.Sinkhole:M.Sinkhole 2.712760                1.938311 3.193975  6e-05

Note that although the -values are quite different, the upper confidence limits are rather consistent!

Adjusting -values from permutation tests is stupid!

Actually, it might not be but one must run, many, many permutations to be sure that -values are closer to true values. The problem is that -values from permutation tests are left-censored. What this means is that a -value that might actually be around can only be as small as if say, permutations are used. Don’t do this! Do not use few permutations and adjust -values!

However, if you adjust (as we did by adjust confidence), this problem does not exist (or at least is not as extreme)! It informs us how large we would expect a test statistic to be if we adjust , which were fairly consistent for our statistics with varied numbers of permutations. This is a better way to go about pairwise tests!

Other reasons not to adjust -values with RRPP

  1. Are we really performing multiple tests? There are some functions out there that are wrappers for vegan::adonis, called something like pairwise_adonis, which perform pairwise tests by subsetting data sets that have 3+ groups into as many two-sample data sets as possible, and re-perform a global ANOVA, restricted to two groups of data. In every one of perhaps many unique tests, unique pooled standard errors are calculated. The total number of permutations is equal to for the groups compared and permutations used. Adjustments of or -values would be smart in these cases. However, RRPP calculates matrices of coefficients for permutations used, which is used to find sets of means, which produce matrices of distances between means. If in one permutation, two means converge, they both might diverge from other means, meaning the pairwise mean distances are not independent in each permutation. The concept for repeating tests and increasing the probability for a type I error is not the same with RRPP! One can think of this as RRPP producing multiple statistics from the same test instead of performing multiple tests.
  2. Effect sizes! Whether something is “significant” is mildly interesting. The size of the effect is more compelling, because it allows on to compare how large a standardized difference between means 1 and 2 is versus 5 and 6, for example. The effect sizes are standard deviates that measure how much greater (or lesser) a statistic is than the expected value from a test where the null hypothesis is true, based on a standard normal sampling distribution. These are simply better than -values.
  3. One should not give into the tyranny of -values. All the concerns with adjudicating -values that has been written, elsewhere, is true here, as well.
  4. Other things you could be doing if you do not set up your analysis to use permutations, run on all available processor cores. Or maybe you need a coffee break?

Concluding remark

If you want to adjust your -values, now you can. We won’t stop you. We will no longer impose our dogma. But as this post has shown, adjusting is smarter, accomplishes the same thing, and provides additional statistics (upper confidence limits) to evaluate.
